prompt: Design GymNova's offer with the Eliminate–Reduce–Raise–Create grid and explain why it could be a blue ocean.
modelAnswer: Eliminate: long contracts, pools, saunas, large machine floors, mirrors and show-off culture. Reduce: opening hours and club size (small neighbourhood studios), number of machines, price (about €35). Raise: personal guidance and coaching, friendliness, convenience (near home/work, no waiting). Create: fixed 30-minute guided circuit sessions, booking via app, community for beginners, maybe tracking of progress. Blue ocean: targets noncustomers (intimidated, time-poor people) rather than competing for existing gym users; lowers costs (small spaces, few machines) while raising value → value innovation, not a niche of the red ocean.
keyPoints: E, R, R, C each with concrete features

prompt: Draw a strategic group map with two dimensions, identify mobility barriers and discuss one empty space.
modelAnswer: Dimensions (example): scope – number of outlets/geographical coverage; resource commitment – quality and vertical integration into roasting. Groups: global chains (many outlets, medium quality), specialty roasters (few outlets, high quality, integrated), bakery chains (many outlets, low quality/price), independents (one outlet, medium/variable). Mobility barriers: brand and capital for many outlets, roasting know-how and sourcing relations for specialty, real-estate access. Empty space: many outlets with specialty-level quality – white space if scalable (e.g. automation, central roasting) or black hole if quality cannot be maintained at scale.
keyPoints: Empty space: white space or black hole

prompt: Locate the industry in its life cycle and explain the consequences for the Five Forces and for a remaining start-up.
modelAnswer: The industry moved from introduction/growth into a shakeout (stagnation, price cuts, exits), heading towards maturity. Consequences: rivalry rises (price competition, overcapacity); buyer power rises – supermarkets concentrate demand and integrate backwards with private labels; threat of entry falls (investors cautious); supplier power (pea protein, co-manufacturers) declines as demand slows. A remaining start-up needs a clear position: cost leadership with scale, or focused differentiation (taste, specific product, food service), or consolidation (merge, become supplier of private labels).
